newsitem.title: DUBAI: Gulf ministers oppose Turkish security belt plan.
newsitem.headline: Gulf ministers oppose Turkish security belt plan.

text.p: Gulf Arab states said they opposed Turkey's plans to create a security belt across the Iraqi border, official Gulf news agencies reported late on Saturday.

"There is a trend not to approve or accept the Turkish desire to set up a security zone inside Iraqi territories if such a zone is created without an official agreement between Iraq and Turkey," the agencies quoted Oman's Minister of State for Foreign Affairs Youssef bin Alawi bin Abdullah as saying.

He was speaking after Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) foreign ministers held talks in Saudi Arabia to unify their response after last week's missile strikes against Iraq by the United States, their key Western ally.
The GCC's Saudi Arabia, Oman, United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Qatar and Kuwait are holding further talks on Sunday and issuing a final statement on their position.
Oman is the current chairman of the oil-rich alliance.

Ankara has said it was preparing to create a security zone just across the Iraqi border to root out bases of Turkish Kurdish rebels fighting for self-rule in southeast Turkey. The plan has received conditional U.S. approval.
Abdullah said the GCC has formed a committee to draw up its position on Iraq, but that Arab states "would not accept any infringement on Iraqi sovereignty."
The GCC is discussing events in northern and southern Iraq, where the U.S. last week fired 44 cruise missiles.
Washington said its strike was a response to the Iraqi army's intervention in northern Iraq to help a Kurdish faction seize a city from a rival group a week ago.
The six GCC states are close allies of the United States, which uses planes from warships in the Gulf and facilities in Saudi Arabia to enforce a no-fly zone up to Iraq's 33rd parallel.

Washington says the wider zone, extended from the 32nd parallel where it was fixed after Iraq's defeat in the 1991 Gulf war, was aimed at further restricting Iraq's ability to pose a threat to its neighbours.
France and Britain are part of the U.S.-led coalition.
"The GCC is with the U.S.-led international coalition...we support the coalition in this regard," Abdullah said.
The GCC was part of the U.S.-led multinational force that ended Iraq's 1990-91 occupation of Kuwait and supported further U.S. action against Iraqi President Saddam Hussein.
